Puzzle 4 · 5 of 10

It remembers nothing

Your chatbot answers the first question well, then forgets it on the second. Or it remembers everything, and each message gets slower and more expensive. Both come from one fact about the API. Here's what your app must send, every time.

  • Puzzle 2: Your first call

    A call to a model is one HTTP POST: a model name, max_tokens (the most it may write), and messages, a list of turns each marked user or assistant. The response holds the continuation, a stop_reason (end_turn when it finished, max_tokens when it was cut off), and usage: the input and output tokens you pay for. Output tokens cost more than input ones, and each one takes time to generate.

The problem

Your first version sends only the user's latest message. The bot answers "What's its battery life?" with "What device do you mean?", though the user named it one message earlier. Your fix sends the whole chat each time, and after fifty messages each reply is slower and costs ten times more. What's going on?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

The Messages API used here is stateless: it does not automatically supply prior turns to a new request. This interface property says nothing about provider logging or data retention. If the model is to "remember" an earlier message, that message must be in this request.

So a chat app keeps the conversation itself, in its ViewModel or database, and chooses the relevant turns for each new message: earlier user messages, earlier answers, then the new message.

Everything in one request, plus the answer the model writes, must fit in the context window: the model's working memory for that request, measured in tokens. Windows are large now, but three things grow with every message:

  • Cost: you pay for all the input tokens again, every turn, so a chat's total cost grows faster than its length. Prompt caching makes a repeated beginning cheaper and faster to read, but you still send it.
  • Time: more input to read before the first token (puzzle 3).
  • Quality: Anthropic notes that as the token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade.

So long chats need a policy: keep the last few turns, replace old ones with a short summary, or drop what doesn't matter. That's your code's decision, not the model's.

The analogy

A brilliant consultant with no memory at all. Every time you call, you read them the whole file so far, then ask your question. A thicker file takes longer to read, costs more of their time, and eventually they skim.

Check yourself

Your app sends only the latest message. Why does the bot forget the device the user just named?

Right. Stateless: send what it should know.

Not quite. The app chose which prior information to include.

Not quite. One message is tiny; the earlier one wasn't in the request.

The app resends its growing full chat history. Why does input usage grow?

Not quite. The price per token is the same; there are just more tokens per request.

Right. A longer input carries more tokens.

Not quite. Possibly, but the cost is mostly the growing input.

What's the difference between the context window and the conversation your app stores?

Not quite. That's the two swapped. Re-read that part ↑

Right. One request's view vs the full record.

Sources
  • Anthropic: Working with the Messages API ("The Messages API is stateless, which means that you always send the full conversational history to the API.")
  • Anthropic: Context windows (the context window is "a 'working memory' for the model"; "As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot")

What you now know

The Messages API example is stateless: the caller supplies whatever prior context this turn needs. Everything sent, plus the answer, must fit in the context window, the model's working memory for that request. Long chats cost more per message and can degrade, so trim, summarise or drop old turns on purpose.
